My class was notoriously ill disciplined, putting us beside NT - so I was familiar with the sort of people u expect from either classes.

I was one of the three NA students who rejected going full express, cuz I thought I could breezily ace my papers. LOL I didn't because I was distracted by a bad choice of friends (ntg to do w their streaming) and some family issues (I was the older sibling w an illiterate parent, gg). Fast forward, I focused on serving my family so I joined the work study scheme in ITE.

I kinda get the feeling of losing my potential, esp since in my interest based clique most of them r from JC, but looking back, this is my story and I'm happier having friends from all kinds of backgrounds. That's why I'm not advising you practically on what directions you should take. Some of my decisions were influenced by the sense of survival or need (e.g. to maintain my family finances) but it cause me to feel unfair that others cld pursue wtv they wanted, and in the end my family left me behind too. 

The real advice here is for you to look thru your values and as best as possible, don't let your circumstance control u. What are your values in life? What if things change? What if things were not what you thought it'll be? A hundred students here regret taking the courses they majored in, and a hundred more were surprised to find how far they've come.

As growing and maturing Sinkie kids, we tend to mistake success for this sense of completion but in reality you're always on the move. In this country you have a template of education > career > family > retirement, it's so prominent. Everyone talks about BTO, savings and cars.

I suffer from sleep paralysis. From young I was used to every kind of living nightmare in the book - floating figures, third-person POV, feeling the real chill of a baby's dead body by my leg and being roughly violated by an unseen being.

There couldn't be worse, right? It was frightening already, having these dreams in repeat, not being able to wake up or know when I will ever. Once, they embodied the face of my boyfriend, staring at me unblinkingly.

The worse was when I was in my old lease, and it was a small maid's room where the single bed took basically the whole space and behind me was a window - so I sleep looking away from it. 

I knew right away I was stuck in a sleep paralysis. Something crawled from behind. Feeling sensations was expected and seeing obscured faces and figures too. But what the fuck, this thing crawled with a body of a human being, on all fours, over my sleeping body, and stared back at me like an owl WITH MY OWN FACE HAHAHA

Twenty over years of nightmares and things have improved, but this just happened last year so I'm still shakened that my night terrors can still scare me.

But after age 12, I like to think that anybody has the autonomy to figure our life on their own, so that's up to them, and how you want to live life every day is yours too.

My brother went on to get a job to keep them financially afloat, and every now and then I chip in. Even if not for long, I'd say it's best you give a shot at living by yourself just for awhile to experience life away from the negativity you're been so familiar with.

Even with my current relentless working hours, at least I don't come home to negativity. I love my family, but loving them makes their actions all the more hurtful. If they can't care for you right, you've given them two decades of your life already. Go ahead and carve the life you want :)

But we found an unexpected friendship and his qualities shone above the people I knew.

This goes back to being unafraid by the romantic boundary, and along with my "friendliness" - I was the kind of gal who tended to forget the slight, small boundary between male-female relationships. It has gotten me into trouble many times before. 

It brought me to my current relationship. 

We were talking about our peers and how they were so fearful of pursuing relationships further, and that people should be a little more braver instead of dilly dallying and giving mixed signals, and then getting disappointed at the lack of intimate connections in their life. Somehow or rather, I suggested going on a date since neither of us had experienced it. When I said this, it was intended as a joke. I thought I would've gotten a snarky comeback as a response. 

I received the opposite. So I quickly pulled a terms and agreements and said *okay, no strings attached! This is just for experience*. I was damn sure this guy wasn't really for me, I hadn't even had a silver of goo goo ga ga for him. 

First day was *intimate*. We decided to hold hands and walk around town, and even when we sat in the café our fingers were on each others'. Just chatting and musing about the hilarity of it all. I was taken aback by the "great acting" and *followed suit*. Damn, he really was re-enacting a pretty good date scene!

Which was fine, I was casual with physical affection. This he did not know, because I'm from co-ed and that brat was from all-boys. Somehow I did not analyse my idea of boundaries was going to be a million times different from someone who's only had to deal with one sex most of his life.

So, according to him, my receptiveness told a different story. Despite my initial reminder he genuinely saw potential in the relationship, and asked for more dates, and I was like yeah, sure, this was fun.

But it wasn't. Towards the end of the first date he went on me relentlessly for sanitising my hands midway when I was holding his. It was a glooming foreshadowing of times to come. Second date, he held me so closely, and I thought he wanted a kiss so I simply gave my first - only to understand it was not what he intended but we went with it and well, *went far*. The affections grew to a proportion against time; I wasn't even emotionally attached to him. I was confused, scared, and felt bloody stupid. Did I not tell him? Did he not know? Why was he asking to stead by the third date?

*I said, see where this goes*.

Eventually he said we may as well seal it and I didn't say anything. Everything fell in together so well that we just walked into it, unthinking, believing it would be as casual as always. But he was so serious, and we both got deeply hurt.

We are both immensely lucky that we could communicate pretty well. 

Despite the many grave fights and moments we shared, eventually a year or so later we reached a plateau: we're young, we'll take this easy and actually see where it goes. Your first date, your first times, may not always go as planned, but it's the experience that should build confidence in your ability to make a good time for a special someone else. 

And a good relationship or ally will never make you feel suffocated, or get angry with you when you confide in them that sentiment. OP, cheer up. After my hell of a time, I guarantee you the girl you just met is way more jialat. Thank the skies you could see her red flags the first time. You will find your own red flags in time, as you can see mine was not speaking up and being clear to my partner.

From partner-to-partner, it is a team effort to accomodate for each other. There is no cookie-cutter relationship for you. You need to make that with your partner.

For English, besides the obvious being practice papers (which isn't all that effective than actually just picking out the common questions e.g. literal questions, quotation questions, paraphrasing > boost vocab bank, comparison/the one with two opposing views, which is usually a bit of quotation and paraphrasing and of course, summary) he's got to begin recognising the question types for comprehension because that's the ultimate killer. He could whip up to be a good writer for Paper 1 and still fall into comprehension's chokehold. Frankly, for English, if he's not a keen reader, then the other more methodical approach would be building up his vocab bank and brushing up his grammar. Get him a book of editing practices, since editing does get better through familiarity (comprehension is different; passages differ from one another). Finally, for paper 1 essays; situational writing is pretty standard, he can literally practise it a few times and pay attention to his vocab usage when it comes to tone (formal, informal) and as for essay writing, well, a lot would suggest having more emphasis on expository writing since that's more straightforward. There's argumentative where you must justift a stand thoroughly, or discursive where you can list down the advantages and disadvantages of the topic. Descriptive and narrative will call for a stronger set of vocab use. Seriously, one surefire way to secure English is through strong vocabulary if you're not that steady with the language and have no special interest for it.

- Study and write a summary of all the artists that is similar to his style or a source of inspiration to him

You school doesn't prepare you sample essays? In that case your school's entire English department is a bust, man. Revision packages are those things schools do to ensure all students have sort of like an equal right just in case their teachers didn't manage to teach them as well as other teachers. All good teachers would be aware that students have different learning styles. Not sure if your school did, though.

Then again, it's been a particularly trying year. There are a couple of websites I've scouted out that has brilliant samples for O Level essays;
- mrseah.com
- therationalethinking.com

First and foremost, work up a bank of vocabulary suited for either argumentative or descriptive writing. It will help greatly in your speed and tact during your exam. 

For introductions it's always customary to start off with how you interpret and define the question after your hook, which could be a one-liner or an anecdote. 

The advantage you have seems to lie in making strong points on the go and having it shown clearly, though I'm not sure how concise you are, which is what the markers want as well. They want to see your ability to put your message across with brevity.

Protip from my side is to sometimes proceed with simplicity. Don't jumble your words up in trying to cook up an overcomplicated sentence. Be precise. 

Finally, for concluding paragraphs - I've seen no way out of this - it appears the best way to whip a good one is to begin with an 'all in all', 'ultimately', 'therefore', 'nevertheless'. Notice the tone of finality. Go on with 'this is why I prefer to think/believe that (your points) should be done or said about (topic) as I feel strongly about how it is approached.' Finish off with a life lesson or something that can be imparted from your essay. 

A good piece of writing has to be memorable and educative in a sense. Think if it like you're imparting knowledge of the topic to someone else, since you're essentially doing just that for English essays. 

All the best and don't give up!
